news.body:
独立游戏发行商PLAYISM宣布：由日本独立游戏开发团队ChaoGames所制作，召唤萌萌兽人的恶魔调教冒险游戏《恶魔连结》Steam版现已推出大型更新！新增了简体中文、繁体中文及英语支持！此外，游戏目前正在进行一周年促销，如今正是购入本作的绝佳机会！
这里是魔法世界玛吉利西亚。身为召唤师的你召唤出了一只恶魔。为了缔结契约，你对他说出了自己的名字，但恶魔却始终不肯报上名号。无奈之下你只能随口以“德比伦”来称呼他。为了帮他实现他的野心——恢复真正的姿态，你需要召唤玛吉利西亚各地的民众，让他们深陷恐惧的漩涡从而收集魔力！
你需要和恶魔“德比伦”一起召唤个性鲜明的角色们。让对方的情绪高涨，将其“感情灵气”转化为魔力进行吸收。
在游戏里，会让你从两个选项中选择其一来刺激对方的情绪。不过这并不是随便乱选就行，你需要活用德比伦的特殊能力——“邪眼洞察”来窥视对方的内心，准确解读对方的想法，从而找出通往正确答案的道路。或许有时候，还能发现对方令人意想不到的一面哦……？

明知这是错误选项，却又忍不住想看看会有什么反应——为了收集结局……做出这种事也是可以的吧？
——嗯，就是这样与恶魔一起做“背德之事”的故事哦。

news.title: Studio Atelico launches Atelico AI Engine into Early Access
news.summary_raw: Studio Atelico has launched its Atelico AI Engine into Early Access.

members.title: Studio Atelico launches Atelico AI Engine into Early Access

news.body:
Studio Atelico launches Atelico AI Engine into Early Access
"The studios that succeed won't be the ones using the most AI, they'll be the ones using AI entirely in service of the player experience," says CEO
Studio Atelico has launched its Atelico AI Engine into Early Access.
The studio's technology, first used in its debut game Bobium Brawlers, is designed to run on-device instead of relying on data centres.
The Atelico AI Engine works with Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, enabling developers to generate images, run language models, implement speech systems, and create AI-driven character behaviors.
The engine allows AI to run alongside gameplay without impacting rendering performance and removes cloud dependencies across Windows, macOS, iOS, and Linux, on both GPU and CPU.
"Until now, developers have had to choose between intelligent gameplay, performance and creative control," said Studio Atelico CEO Piero Molino.
"We built the Atelico AI Engine so studios don't have to make those trade-offs. The studios that succeed won't be the ones using the most AI, they'll be the ones using AI entirely in service of the player experience."
Developers interested in Studio Atelico's technology can request access through the company's website.
Earlier this year, GamesIndustry.biz spoke with Studio Atelico about how it used its technology to develop Bobium Brawlers, a project designed to showcase the engine.
"Our long-term aim would be to be the Epic Games of AI," Molino told us. "Where you both do games that are made possible by new technology, and then the technology helps create new games. It's a self-reinforcing loop."
Molino and chief product officer Chris Olson also discussed how the company's AI-first ecosystem leverages generative AI trained on its artists' work.
"We're not looking to reduce steps in the workflow so that you can fire half your art team," said Olson. "We have an art director. We pay our artists. We recently just released a document that's in draft form, but it hints at where we want to go, called ARC, the Artist Rights Contract, and it's so that an artist can use this as a way to interact and protect their livelihood and their art."
"It allows them to define what their art can be used for, gives them a chance to participate in the upside if their art is trained on the models, and very specific use cases. It's only used for this game. You have to renegotiate if you're going to use the art for other purposes."
Molino added: "Because we train our own models for doing these things on our own art and our own, in this case, our own decks being created in-house, so it's our own data. We are doing it ethically; we're not replacing anyone here. We are just creating something that would not have been possible before with data that we own."

members.title: Diablo-Style PvP by Former Blizzard CCO Is Coming to Early Access in November

news.body:
Diablo-Style PvP by Former Blizzard CCO Is Coming to Early Access in November
Arkheron is Bonfire Studios' first game.
Arkheron, a fast-paced isometric PvP game by Bonfire Studios, will arrive in early access on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S on November 27. Prepare your friends because you'll be one of the 15 teams of three to fight to ascend a mysterious tower.
There are no heroes or roles; your strategy depends on communication and the items you collect. The developers promise "a hundred ways a fight can turn" and unique runs every time, thanks to an abundance of Relics that dramatically change the play and give you exciting abilities.
"Arkheron's isometric free-aim combat keeps you locked into the fight: swivel to line up a shot, dodge in close, and read the danger through sound and positioning before you see it. It plays the same on a controller as it does on mouse and keyboard — so if your friends are on console, you're not choosing between playing with them and playing well."
Bonfire Studios
You start against another team and carve your way up to meet in Ascension, where 15 teams fight monsters and rival squads. The field gets smaller every floor, like in a battle royale, until one team is left standing.
If the visuals remind you of Diablo, there is a reason: Bonfire Studios was founded by Rob Pardo, former Chief Creative Officer of Blizzard, who teamed up with other Blizzard veterans and former Nexon America CEO Min Kim to release Arkheron as the studio's first game later this year.
Bonfire Studios
"We have a game we love. Arkheron creates the kind of wild, memorable player stories that only happen here, and we're excited to open it up to more players. It's still in development and a long way from the competitive experience we want it to be at 1.0. Early Access gives more players the chance to play while we keep cooking. We want to gather meaningful feedback, iterate alongside the community, and be transparent about what we're working on," the studio said.
The game will leave early access when "it’s earned a place at the top of your gaming rotation." news.title: Roblox growth slumps, but the company is betting big on AI to compensate
news.summary_raw: Roblox's quarterly financial results missed their daily active user goals, but the company plans to make up for it somehow with AI.

members.title: Roblox growth slumps, but the company is betting big on AI to compensate
Roblox Q3 results beat expectations despite bookings falling 12% to $1.7bn

news.body:
Roblox reported its quarterly financial results yesterday and the numbers are a little mixed. While the company fell well short of the daily active user goals and guidance, leadership believes that generative AI will be the silver bullet that makes up for the decline in users.
Despite viral games like You Can Steal an Egg making waves on Roblox this past quarter, daily active users fell 9 percent year over year and well below the 145 million estimate at just 138 million. The company did beat estimates in hours engaged at 34 billion, but that still represents a 15 percent decline from the previous year. From the financial release, Roblox attributed this declination to the previous year representing strong growth.
The company plans to offset this lesser demand, however, by heavily investing in generative AI game creation initiatives. Roblox states that over 80% of the platform's top 100 games from the past quarter are made using AI tools.
Roblox's AI training process drew attention this earlier week after the company confirmed to Game Developer that an AI agent had scraped 145.5 GB of 3D assets, including adult content, from Open3DLab. A Roblox spokesperson characterized this as a mistake, saying that the content would not be used for AI training in the future.
Founder and CEO David Baszucki remained bullish on AI in comments to investors. "AI is fundamentally reshaping the gaming industry, driving a step function change in the pace at which content can be created," he said.

members.title: 生软联合创始人：EA高管没做过游戏，关闭工作室不是意外
Report: EA shut down BioWare in favor of Star Wars: Battlefront sequel after previously decrying licensed games

news.body:
“在埃德蒙顿，生软曾经像一座象征着希望、活力和无限可能的灯塔，向世人证明了尽管这座城市历史上并不以游戏闻名，当地开发者仍有能力打造出非同凡响的作品。”
上周三，当生软（BioWare）“死亡”的消息传开时，57岁的格雷格·泽舒克（Greg Zeschuk）正在加拿大不列颠哥伦比亚省中部的巴宾河河边垂钓虹鳟。为了专心钓鱼，泽舒克关掉了手机。那天晚些时候，泽舒克从河边回到度假小屋，才发现手机里涌入了一连串短信。“我收到了差不多10条短信。”泽舒克说，“我刚打开手机，就看到有人发消息向我表示慰问：‘我对生软的遭遇深感遗憾。’当时我的第一反应就是：‘生软没了！’”
1995年，泽舒克和雷·穆齐卡、奥古斯汀·叶共同创办了生软。过去30年间，生软打造了《博德之门》《质量效应》《龙腾世纪》等多款备受推崇的游戏，甚至重新定义了角色扮演品类。作为生软联合创始人，泽舒克和穆齐卡还在2018年底被授予“加拿大勋章”。然而，EA近期宣布将关闭生软，终止“质量效应”系列新作的早期开发工作，并裁掉工作室剩余的大约50名员工。这是EA裁员重组计划中的一部分：在EA被沙特牵头的财团以550亿美元收购的私有化交易完成短短78天后，这家发行商就启动了一轮涉及约400人的裁员。
据泽舒克透露，过去几天他曾婉拒其他媒体的采访请求，与笔者对话是他首次就生软被关闭一事发表看法。“我没有第一时间感受到强烈的情感冲击。”泽舒克说，“我不在现场，没有亲身经历那一刻。但换个角度来看，这其实挺好，因为我可以更从容地接受和消化上周发生的一切……当然，生软被关闭确实令人感到难过、痛苦。在埃德蒙顿，生软曾经像一座象征着希望、活力和无限可能的灯塔，向世人证明了尽管这座城市历史上并不以游戏闻名，当地开发者仍有能力打造出非同凡响的作品。”
从某种意义上讲，早在14年前，当泽舒克和穆齐卡在同一个月离开游戏行业时，他俩已经体会了失去生软的痛苦。“我在很久很久以前就感受了所有情绪。要想以健康的方式离开一家公司，我必须切断情感羁绊，从情绪中抽离出来并告诉自己：‘好了，情感抒发完毕，现在是时候往前看了。’”泽舒克补充，“与生软被关闭相比，我更为那些失去工作的人感到担忧。如今游戏行业的竞争无比残酷，对任何从业者来说，被迫踏上求职之路都是一件相当可怕的事情。”
有人或许认为，从2007年生软被EA收购的那一刻起，这家加拿大工作室就已经注定会走下坡路。但泽舒克本人并不这么看。2013年1月，彼时已离开生软数月的泽舒克在一次采访中告诉笔者：“我认为，生软之所以能够在EA获得成功，原因之一是我们公司足够成熟，有足够优秀的人才来应对EA的‘熊抱’——一种出于好意，却常常用力过猛的拥抱。我们需要足够坚韧才能挺过来，我想我们做到了。在此过程中，我们也会不断成长和蜕变。”
如今回头来看，面对EA“熊抱”，生软的态度是否随着时间推移变得越来越软，直至彻底屈服？泽舒克表示，EA在他离职后为生软提供了数次机会，开发《龙腾世纪：影障守护者》是最后一次。“生软证明了自己能够在既定框架内运作，并成功推出了几款产品。令人感到遗憾的是，当EA被收购后，他们再也没有机会制作下一款‘质量效应’游戏了。”
按照泽舒克的说法，他和穆齐卡之所以将生软卖给EA（译注：奥古斯汀·叶已于1998年离开生软），并非因为工作室陷入了困境。泽舒克补充，他从不为这个决定感到后悔。“那会儿生软的整体状况很好，没人强迫我们出售工作室，我们也没有受到任何外部压力。不过，考虑到奥斯汀团队主导的‘星球大战’项目需要更多资金，而且规模更大的公司能给我们带来稳定性，我们主动寻求改变。”他说，“归根结底，我们可能过早迈出了这一步，但我们确实认为，与其独自承担经营生软的所有风险，倒不如投靠一家大公司。”
“事实上，当时有多种选择摆在我们面前，我觉得我们从中找到了最佳选项。尽管生软的发展前景看起来还不错，但经过权衡，我们认为加入一个更大的平台更稳妥。”
与许多其他游戏公司的创始人一样，泽舒克在从行业退休后的几年里曾经远离游戏。后来，他又重新爱上了游戏，却几乎从来不玩生软在他离开后推出的任何作品。“我在《圣歌》里逛悠过，但从来没玩过《质量效应：仙女座》。”泽舒克透露，“经过几年的‘冷静期’后，我重拾这份爱好，现在算是一名重度玩家。”
随着年龄增长，泽舒克对游戏的喜好也发生了转变：他不再像年轻时那么喜欢剧情向游戏，而是更偏爱“基于攻击性”的游戏。例如，泽舒克自称花了大把时间玩“仁王”系列游戏，并兴致勃勃地聊起了他在《仁王2》中通关高难度挑战模式奈落狱的经历。“我在那个模式里恐怕就投入了超过1200个小时……我真心喜欢动作对战类型的游戏，或许这就是我们当年决定立项开发《翡翠帝国》的原因。”泽舒克说，“我还是《艾尔登法环》的铁杆粉丝，觉得它很可能是史上最伟大的游戏。当然，《塞尔达传说》也十分接近。”
谈到生软在过去十几年里的变化，泽舒克指出，任何工作室都不可能突然大变样，而是会经历渐进的演变过程。在他看来，生软曾经拥有浓厚的创业公司气质，但这种气质在生软被EA收购、几位创始人离开后逐渐消失了。“随着创始团队成员纷纷离开，新人加入，工作室自然会发生变化。”他解释，“我不会狂妄到认为我和穆齐卡是生软的灵魂人物，仿佛我俩一走，工作室就要完蛋了。事实绝非如此。当我俩离开时，生软拥有一支人才济济的强大团队，完全能够填补我俩留下的空缺。然而，改变总会悄悄发生。”
今年8月，当泽舒克听说EA被沙特公共投资基金牵头的财团收购时，他就隐隐预感到，生软的结局恐怕不会太好。“我觉得那就像钉在棺材上的最后一颗钉子。”泽舒克说，“从某种意义上讲，EA又一次变得与过去完全不同。虽然我没有听说任何内部消息，但我推测，EA背后的财团只想要那些体育游戏和‘战地’系列，其他一切都无关紧要。生软制作的游戏比较独特，往往结构复杂、开发周期漫长。相比之下，每年推出体育游戏系列的新品容易得多，并且也更赚钱。”
当EA宣布关闭生软时，《网络奇兵》《杀出重围》主创、现已退休的游戏设计师沃伦·斯派克特（Warren Spector）在职场社交平台领英上的一则帖子中罕见爆粗，声称EA应解雇做出这个“狗屁”决定的高管，而非一线开发者。作为生软联合创始人，泽舒克的反应反倒更加冷静克制。“老实说，这已经与我无关。早在15年前，我就不得不在情感上与生软彻底切割……我认为‘断舍离’有益身心，如果不迈出这一步，我恐怕会永远陷入自我怀疑，并始终在原地徘徊。”
尽管如此，泽舒克承认，他对游戏行业对待开发者的方式感到不满。按照泽舒克的说法，生软等工作室之所以曾经获得成功，在很大程度上依赖于多年来潜心打磨技艺，并默契配合的团队成员，然而，掌握决策权的高管们却低估了团队的重要性。“许多高管想当然地以为随便找一群人组队，再加上AI，就能创作出伟大的游戏作品。这种观念太荒谬，太外行了。”泽舒克说，“另一个残酷现实是：在几乎所有游戏公司，那些管理者往往没有开发游戏的一线经验……他们从来没有参与过一款游戏的完整制作过程，所以根本不了解游戏开发究竟是怎么一回事。”
很多玩家想知道，泽舒克是否对回购生软工作室的名称和“质量效应”IP感兴趣？泽舒克对此回应：“不，多年前我已经离开游戏行业，从来没有打算回归。我对以玩家的身份体验游戏感到开心。尽管我对如何制作游戏有自己的见解，这个想法听起来也很诱人，但只要想到为了制作一款出色的游戏需要倾注多少心血，付出多大代价，我就觉得不值得。我绝对不可能走回头路。”
当然，泽舒克也不会把自己的所有时间都用来钓鱼。2017年，泽舒克在埃德蒙顿创办了酿酒厂Blind Enthusiasm Brewing Company。经过几年的发展，如今Blind Enthusiasm已经成为一家“大型精品酒厂”，拥有十几名员工，每年生产6万到10万瓶（每瓶750毫升）啤酒。这家酿酒厂的产品远销海外，包括美国、欧洲和日本，在不久后的未来还将进入中国市场。“酿酒厂生意不错，这是我的新事业。如今回想起在游戏行业经历过的前尘往事，我既不感伤，也不怀念。对我来说，人生中的那个章节早已翻篇。”

members.title: 狙击猴模范降临：《气球塔防》57版本国服正式上线

news.body:
10月30日，让广大玩家翘首以盼的《气球塔防6》57国服版本终于到来，不仅为玩家带来了全新模范猴——狙击模范「S.P.I.D.E.R 蜘蛛猴」，更有关于模范能量、Insta猴收集的系统性更新，可谓份量满满。
伫立在视野毫无遮挡的高耸瞭望塔顶，「S.P.I.D.E.R 蜘蛛猴」可通过精准瞄准系统，将战场视野共享给其他狙击猴。玩家可以将其他狙击手猴设置为“跟随指令”（集中火力攻击蜘蛛猴的目标），也可以让它们自由开火。
蜘蛛猴的主攻击会发射威力强劲的大口径子弹，并在命中气球后向外溅射弹片，在短暂的延迟后，弹片将如烟花般呼啸而过，飞向附近的气球，爆炸并造成范围伤害。
它的基础射速较慢，但气球越靠近终点，射速就会越快。若持续攻击同一目标，射速还可以得到进一步的提升。
一技能军备切换，开启技能后可以召唤弹药补给，将不会再有设计次数限制，同时还会强化附近的狙击手猴，为应对密集的气球大军提供输出保障。
二技能正午狙杀，则是对BOSS的特攻神技。开启后。蜘蛛猴将会停止子弹攻击，直接锁定场上血量最高的目标并蓄力发射强力射弹，蓄力时间越长，伤害则越高，蓄力全满后，将会释放毁灭性的一击，足以击穿BOSS级气球或是直接秒杀目标。
伴随着蜘蛛猴的加入，狙击手猴的空投补给能力也同步进行了调整与强化，在蜘蛛猴的加持下，「弹药补给」会强化接下来的攻击，可使接下来的数次攻击附带爆炸效果，也可以切换到「现金补给」能力，迅速在回合内补充经济。
可以看出，狙击猴模范与《气球塔防6》的大多数模范的设计理念完全不同，它摈弃了全能通杀型的一夫当关万夫莫开模式，转而成为对单体的特攻模范和一定的辅助效果。80万的昂贵造价，蓄力一枪的血条消失术，注定了它是无尽模式以及活动关卡中的BOSS杀器。
Insta猴作为通关时的临时助力，对玩家素有帮助。过去，获取Insta猴除了每日宝箱和100回合奖励等免费渠道外，商店内的购买包是随机购买性质，固定刷新2只随机T1、2只随机T2、1只随机T3。
在更新后的新系统中，随机内购包被彻底移除，玩家补全图鉴不再被运气阻挡。新系统提供9个指定的单体Insta猴，外加1个预组捆绑包，所有玩家看到的列表完全一致，每两周整租刷新一次。
玩家可以在完成对应游玩目标后用猴币购买，不必再抽盲盒拼运气。
除此之外，“精选”页面还将加入全新的自由模式挑战。在英雄选择和防御塔总数受限的情况下，通关指定回合完成挑战目标，即可解锁特别宝箱，包含3个Insta猴奖励，其中2个选项由个人收集进度定制，玩家可在其中任选其一。
57版本的全新地图，来自于玩家社区的创作——「夺船大战」。
晴空万里，顺风航行，海盗气球会从左右两侧对玩家展开接舷战，玩家需要阻止它们突袭船长室，偷走珍贵的战利品。
这张地图的设计小巧思在于，玩家在中期还可以选择合适的时机，拆掉中间的木板区域，这将给玩家增加空间自由布置水上防御。
当然，也可以不管不顾，在木板的狭小区域构筑陆地防御。
另外，社区翘首以盼的大师模式终于以“精通模式任务”更新在任务模块中。玩家需要用一半的经济，挑战更强大的敌人，这势必会带来十足的挑战性。
除了上述较大的更新内容之外，自然也少不了每一次更新都不会缺席的细节更新以及平衡性调整。诸如僵尸萨乌达的棺材放置动画、村庄海盗旗帜以及经典的瞄准头像……这样的细节优化，似乎永远都不会止步。
除此之外，新一期的万圣节极速狂欢活动中，玩家只需要挑战关卡获取星星，便可以免费获得定制的万圣节外观。
同时商城中还同步上线了万圣节限定皮肤的奖杯商店，每一个获得的奖杯除了是实力的象征，也可以切切实实为玩家谋取奖励。
琳琅满目的更新不禁让人感慨，不知不觉，《气球塔防》已然长久运营了这么多年，猴村居然还有这么多推陈出新的空间。一张新地图、一个新模范、几行平衡性改动，都能让玩家感受到亲切的陪伴感，更多的惊喜只有亲自上手玩一玩才能切身感受到。
这一次更新，不妨让我们一起再度动动手指，戳戳气球，找回曾经的快乐吧！

members.title: 2026 Industry releases and what’s coming in Q4

news.body:
2026 Industry releases and what’s coming in Q4
Avery Vernon-Moore - Unity Technologies
2026 has been a big year for Unity Industry, so we're looking back at the major Unity Industry releases and updates, plus a preview on what’s coming in Q4.
In March, Unity Studio made it possible to create interactive 3D experiences directly in a web browser. By September, robotics teams could prototype and validate systems in simulation before deploying them to physical hardware. In between, Unity Industry shipped 15+ releases.
Those releases span every part of the Unity Industry product suite. They serve teams building digital twins, simulations, HMI and embedded systems, robotics, XR training, and product configurators.
TL;DR: Unity Industry's 2026 releases at a glance
Short on time? Here's what Unity Industry shipped this year:
- AI agents joined the 3D data pipeline: Industry AI Workflows launched in October as an experimental release, so your own AI agent can prep, optimize, and publish CAD data across Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, and Pipeline Automation.
- Design and simulation tools connected to Unity: The experimental UI Toolkit Connector for Figma turns Figma frames into editable Unity UI, and the Unity USD Toolkit round-trips USD between Unity and NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
- 3D creation moved into the browser: Unity Studio went GA in March, then added annotations, Editor export, and live co-editing.
- Collaboration opened up beyond the Editor: Unity Pipeline entered closed beta, giving every role one API into a Unity production.
- Enterprise security got independent proof: Unity's creator services are now SOC 2 Type 2 certified, and Asset Manager deploys in your own cloud.
- Robotics and embedded got purpose-built tools: Simulation Pro entered early access. Automotive teams got multi-window control and a shared Android render service.
- The Editor kept getting faster: Unity 6.4, 6.5, and 6.6 shipped, with Unity 6.7 LTS coming soon.
Below, we break down every Unity Industry release from 2026 by quarter and product, then preview what's coming in Q4.
Q1 2026: 3D creation opens up
Unity Studio is generally available
Bring 3D ideas to life, fast: Unity Studio is a web-based editor that lets anyone build and share interactive 3D apps. No coding and no installs. Import your 3D data, add interactivity, and share a link for review.
Unity 6.4
6.4 brought faster scene building, smoother workflows, and ECS now built into the Editor: The release integrated Project Auditor, moved ECS packages into the core Editor release cycle, and expanded rendering, input, and platform support.
Q2 2026: From solo tool to team workspace
Unity Studio: releases for connected collaboration
- Custom Transformations: More control over 3D imports. Choose optimized or full hierarchy, and keep animations and structure without external tools.
- Studio to Editor Export: Start fast, scale without rebuilding. Send Studio projects to the Unity Editor with assets, UI, and logic intact. Watch it
- Annotations: Feedback where it matters. Pin comments and replies to the exact spot in a 3D scene. Watch it
- Real-time Collaboration: Create together in real time. Co-edit shared 3D scenes live, with presence and comments built in. Watch it
Read more about Studio collaboration and Editor export
Unity Asset Manager: Self-Hosted Deployment
Deployment in your cloud: Deploy Asset Manager directly to your private cloud. Keep sensitive 3D data in your own environment while you automate heavy prep.
Unity 6.5 and embedded multi-window support
- Unity 6.5: Faster workflows, stronger foundations. Performance, graphics, 2D, and platform gains across Android, Apple, Web, and Nintendo Switch 2, plus groundwork for CoreCLR. Read the launch post
- GameWindow multi-window support: Granular, runtime control over every window. Create, arrange, and control multiple Unity windows across one or more displays, built for automotive cockpits and industrial control panels. Read the documentation.
Q3 2026: Trust, skills, and new frontiers
Unite Seoul set the pace for the quarter. Read the recap
Platform: open and verified
- Unity Pipeline enters closed beta: Open your Unity production to the whole team. A unified API connects every role and tool, including DCCs, IDEs, the CLI, and supported AI agents. No Editor seat required. Apply for the beta
- SOC 2 Type 2 certification: Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, Studio, Pipeline, and DevOps are SOC 2 Type 2 certified, audited by Coalfire. Visit the Trust Center
Unity Academy Pro
Scale Unity skills across teams: Structured, role-based training for industrial teams, so they onboard faster and work more efficiently. Explore Academy Pro
Robotics: Simulation Pro early access
Simulate robotics workflows in Unity: Prototype, test, and validate robots, sensors, and AI before deployment, with ROS-connected tools. Run on private clouds or local servers, with no hardware lock-in.
Embedded and HMI: Unity Render Service now in Beta
One Unity instance, shared across every Android app: Android applications can connect to a shared Unity runtime, reducing startup time and resource duplication compared with running a separate Unity instance for each app.
Unity 6.6
Build smoother, deploy further: Fast Enter Play Mode, faster asset loading with Content Directories, a new Hierarchy window, and reach to Android XR devices such as XREAL AURA. Read about Android XR glasses support
UI Toolkit Connector for Figma (experimental)
Your Figma file becomes real Unity UI: Push Figma frames into Unity as editable UI Toolkit documents and pick up where design left off in UI Builder. Your design system comes with you: Figma variables carry over as themes, such as Dark and Light, and components become working Unity controls. Supported style and layout edits made in Unity can be pushed back to Figma manually or automatically, so design and build stay in sync. This is an early release and we’d love your feedback as we shape the product. Get the Figma plugin
Q4 2026 Preview
Now available: Industry AI Workflows (experimental)
Weeks of prep work, done in hours: Connect your own AI agent to Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, and Pipeline Automation. Describe the outcome you want, and the agent builds the whole workflow. Point it at a STEP file and it imports, repairs, optimizes, QA-renders, exports, publishes, tags, and versions the result.
- Use the agent you already have: Works with Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, so models stay under your existing AI policy.
- Pipelines by description: Author, validate, trigger, and monitor Pipeline Automation jobs without writing JSON by hand.
- Fast to set up: Install with two commands and one browser login. Run on public Unity Cloud or a self-hosted deployment.
- No new SKU: Runs on the Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, and Pipeline Automation entitlements you already have.
Industry AI Workflows is an experimental release. Try AI Workflows today
Unity USD Toolkit (experimental)
Round-trip USD between Unity and Isaac Sim: Bring OpenUSD workflows into Unity. Read, write, and round-trip USD stages used in simulation pipelines, with hierarchy and metadata intact. Live scene sync keeps object positions, rotations, and scales aligned between Unity and NVIDIA Isaac Sim in real time. Prototype robotics workflows, validate digital twins, or iterate on synthetic data scenes without manual re-exports.
This is an experimental release. Try it and tell us what your simulation team needs next. Explore the USD Toolkit
Coming later this quarter
This section describes features and timing still in development. These reflect our current plans, and availability could change.
Editor agent plugins (beta)
Official Unity plugins for Claude, Codex and Grok give AI agents Unity-built skills for common development tasks. Agents check your project, use the current API and verify results before handing work back. Skills are developed and maintained by specialist Unity teams, so you can expect better output and fewer coding errors. Kimi and Antigravity plugins coming later this year.
Asset Manager Folder sharing
Open the right folder to the right people. Share nested folders with specific people and set a role for each folder, so collaborators go straight to the assets they need.
Asset Manager Collection sharing
Protect the project, share the collection. Give external partners and agencies access to one collection of assets while the rest of your repository stays private.
Unity 6.7 LTS
Build confidently for the long term. The next Long Term Support release brings a year of Unity 6 performance and workflow gains to teams shipping at scale.
Which Unity Industry release should you explore first?
Start with the release that's costing you time:

- Testing robots on real hardware? Ask us about Simulation Pro early access.

news.summary_raw: This new retro fantasy RPG blends King’s Field-style first-person exploration with Dark Souls-inspired combat, more than 50 weapons, 100 enemies, hidden secrets, and an unusual flying sword.

members.title: This New Retro Fantasy Indie RPG Channels Dark Souls and King's Field

news.body:
This New Retro Fantasy Indie RPG Channels Dark Souls and King's Field
This new retro fantasy RPG blends King’s Field-style first-person exploration with Dark Souls-inspired combat, more than 50 weapons, 100 enemies, hidden secrets, and an unusual flying sword.
In case you missed it
Queen's Domain Info
Freshly Baked Games and Future Friends Games have officially launched Queen’s Domain, a first-person fantasy action RPG inspired by the earliest FromSoftware games.
Available now for PC via Steam, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and Nintendo Switch 2, Queen’s Domain sends players to the mysterious Isle of Neasied in search of their missing father. Unfortunately, the island is filled with monsters, concealed paths, powerful bosses, and an ancient Queen beginning to awaken.
The first-person perspective, chunky retro visuals, deliberate swordplay, and interconnected environments immediately evoke King’s Field and Shadow Tower. Its action-oriented combat incorporates more recognizable Soulslike elements, including stamina management, charge attacks, weapon-specific abilities, character leveling, and dangerous encounters where careless aggression can quickly prove fatal.
Queen’s Domain introduces some distinctive ideas of its own. Players wield the Legendary Holy Sword Endu, which doubles as a traversal tool capable of carrying its owner through the air. Upgrades gradually extend the sword’s flight distance, opening new paths across the island and turning vertical exploration into an important part of progression.
The full game contains more than 50 upgradable melee weapons, over 20 types of secondary throwing weapons, and upwards of 100 enemies, minibosses, and bosses. Players can improve their attributes using experience points and gain additional statistical bonuses by discovering and eating food.
Its labyrinthine world is designed as a single interconnected space filled with shortcuts and hidden areas rather than a sequence of isolated levels. Exploring thoroughly may reveal equipment, upgrades, and routes that make later encounters more manageable, preserving the sense of mystery that defined FromSoftware’s early dungeon crawlers.
Queen’s Domain was created by Freshly Baked Games, a two-person independent studio founded by developers Eric and Bradley. Development began in mid-2023, drawing upon the pair’s shared appreciation for FromSoftware, The Legend of Zelda, anime, and retro fantasy games.
Interest grew rapidly following the game’s reveal and playable demo. Queen’s Domain accumulated more than 300,000 Steam wishlists. Within its first few hours, Queen’s Domain surpassed 3,500 concurrent Steam players, with 118 user reviews averaging 'Very Positive ' so far. Those figures will naturally continue changing as more players begin its estimated 40-hour adventure.

news.title: New Halloween Game Put Original Michael Myers Actor in a Mocap Suit
news.summary_raw: IllFonic CCO Jared Gerritzen discusses recreating 1978 Haddonfield, capturing Nick Castle’s original Michael Myers movements, using UE5 lighting, and building reactive NPC systems for Halloween: The Game.

members.title: New Halloween Game Put Original Michael Myers Actor in a Mocap Suit

news.body:
New Halloween Game Put Original Michael Myers Actor in a Mocap Suit
IllFonic CCO Jared Gerritzen discusses recreating 1978 Haddonfield, capturing Nick Castle’s original Michael Myers movements, using UE5 lighting, and building reactive NPC systems for Halloween: The Game.
IllFonic has spent much of the past decade refining its approach to asymmetrical multiplayer through games including Friday the 13th: The Game, Predator: Hunting Grounds, and Ghostbusters: Spirits Unleashed. Halloween: The Game applies those lessons to one of horror’s most influential films, but its recreation of Haddonfield involves considerably more than placing Michael Myers inside another familiar multiplayer formula.
Released on September 8 for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S, the game combines a standalone single-player story with 1v4 multiplayer matches set across a town populated by reactive NPCs. Civilian players must protect Haddonfield’s residents, arm them, and alert the police, while Michael uses darkness, stealth, and supernatural abilities to hunt them.
Unlike the empty competitive arenas found in many asymmetrical games, its maps are intended to feel like functioning neighborhoods disrupted by the arrival of The Shape. We spoke with IllFonic Chief Creative Officer Jared Gerritzen about translating the original film’s lenses, camera movement, lighting, clothing, and distinctly 1970s suburban aesthetic into an interactive space.
Check out the game's website for more info about it.
Halloween: The Game is based specifically on the original 1978 film. From an art and production standpoint, how did the team approach translating that film’s visual language into a playable horror sandbox?
Jared Gerritzen, IllFonic COO: The best part was we had such a great place to start with the movie, from the clothing and hairstyles down to the camera styles, including the lenses, and the steadicam movement was all so well documented. What was not expected was teaching the team what the 70s looked like.
Some of them had not been born yet, haha. I’m lucky I was born during this aesthetic period, so I grew up in that era. I never thought I would have to talk so much about my childhood decor and memories. Something as funny as telling the devs about lawn darts, and how to play with us kids throwing them straight in the air and running. If you walk through the game locations, you will see the team did a great job, taking the look and feel from the film, my childhood descriptions, and online searches, applying all to the final product really well.
Haddonfield is such an ordinary-looking place on screen, which is part of what makes the film frightening. How did you design environments that feel suburban, familiar, and grounded while still supporting stealth, pursuit, exploration, and multiplayer readability?
Jared Gerritzen: I mean, we really needed to make everything feel like it could happen in any town; that is what Haddonfield needs to be. It was a really good test of self-control to make everything so normal. The art and design team really did an amazing job of making it feel like so many places in America. It could be anywhere that anyone has been before. I can point to some parts of the map that feel like where any of our company offices are located.
The game is powered by Unreal Engine 5, highlighting realistic visuals, cinema-quality lighting, lifelike NPCs, and dynamic gameplay systems. What did UE5 enable for this project, especially in terms of lighting, atmosphere, materials, animation, and performance?
Jared Gerritzen: The dynamic lighting in UE5 was the biggest evolution that I think was so great to work with. For years we’ve been using baked lighting that cannot change mid-match. Getting dynamic lighting that we can ship with was amazing.
Now we can finally have the game change its lighting, affect large areas with power boxes, and do really cool new lighting for the Shapejump world Michael moves through.
Michael Myers has a very specific screen presence: slow, deliberate, almost emotionless, but still terrifying. How did the animation team capture that physicality while making him feel responsive and readable as a playable character?
Jared Gerritzen: We lucked out and got to work with Nick Castle from the start; we even got him in a mocap suit to get his actual movements. The animation team also got to speak with him and the IP holders about his movement and how he might kill.
Also, this team really gave a lot of feedback, and we watched all the movies a lot.
What do you think specifically sets this game apart from the likes of Dead by Daylight and Texas Chainsaw Massacre, or the upcoming Saw game? Or even your own previous games like Friday the 13th and Predator?
Jared Gerritzen: It’s the NPC and AI interaction in the world; in all the other games, you only need to worry about yourself.
In Halloween: The Game, we wanted to take the Hero and let you truly be the hero of the town. You need to try to save people and do a lot more than run routes over and over. Cops coming into the maps that the killed players can take control over to help pressure a bloodthirsty Michael at the end also really changes things up throughout the matches.
Can you walk us through the production pipeline for one key character or environment, from film reference and concept work to modeling, texturing, rigging, animation, lighting, VFX, and final implementation?
Jared Gerritzen: Oh, you mean the hard part of the game. I’ve worked on a lot of titles but Halloween has some of the biggest fans so we knew we had to get this right.
We would concept a character, get that approved and/or iterate based on feedback, then build the model in 3D, get that approved, then texture, get that approved, and then build the hair. This is me overly simplifying it all. A lot of work went into the Michaels and heroes, but they needed to be perfect and capture the era and do right by a truly epic film.
Asymmetrical horror games depend heavily on sound, sightlines, pacing, and player uncertainty. How do the design, audio, art, and level teams work together to create tension without making matches feel unfair or confusing?
Jared Gerritzen: A lot of playtesting is key to what drives development. IllFonic is always doing playtests, giving feedback, and capturing data. But this is also our fifth asymmetrical game, and we have a lot of theories and lessons we follow.
We have figured these out over the last decade. We really are not a huge studio that is slow-moving. We circle up all the time with the right people to get systems figured out fast and test them to make sure it is right, as much as we can. It’s what lets us also keep working post-launch to do patches and add more content pretty quickly.
The game includes both a standalone single-player story and dynamic asymmetrical multiplayer matches. How do you build maps, NPC behavior, and systems that can support both authored horror moments and unpredictable multiplayer encounters?
Jared Gerritzen: When we first talked about Halloween: The Game being made, the first thing we all decided was you needed to be the Hero. The player needed to save NPCs, and that helped us reinforce the idea of adding a single-player component.
We also have experience in past games, learning the need for NPCs to give the game more random moments to experience. We add as much as we can to make the game dynamic and have uncommon moments that players do not get in every match. I love watching gamers clip insane moments and having a blast. The NPCs are key and also really help other skill sets of players that might not be hyper-multiplayer skilled.
IllFonic has a long history with asymmetrical multiplayer horror. What lessons from previous projects most directly shaped Halloween: The Game, and where did this IP force the team to rethink its usual approach?
Jared Gerritzen: Really, the biggest lesson we have learned, and it got even more reinforced with this project, is we need to continue to choose IPs that we really are fans of ourselves. We also know we cannot make a great game without a solid idea from day one of what it will be. We have been offered a lot of IPs, and we’ve toyed with the idea of doing huge IPs, but if we cannot see a game in it, we won’t touch it.
The short answer is doing what we know to be a core building block for us as a company and keep doing it better each time.
Jared Gerritzen, IllFonic COO
Interview conducted by David Jagneaux

news.title: Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
news.summary_raw: Update: Anthropic has confirmed it's released an update to Opus 5.5 to "steer" Claude Code away from "recreating someone else's specific game."

members.title: Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games

news.body:
Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
Update: Anthropic has confirmed it's released an update to Opus 5.5 to "steer" Claude Code away from "recreating someone else's specific game."
It appears Anthropic may be (quietly) taking action to stem the flood of AI-driven game remakes that have hit the video game industry in the last few month, which saw users creating their own versions of classic and upcoming games, sometimes for fun, sometimes for financial gain.
Earlier today X (formerly Twitter) user Chasm said that they spotted an update to Claude Code's "rules" that was pushed sometime on October 27. The rule is listed under "tengu_heron_brook," and reads "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Do not build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." Chasm reports that there is no way to disable the rule.
An Anthropic spokesperson referred us to a statement by Anthropic member of technical staff Addy Osmani also posted on X. "We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Osmani wrote. "Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance."
"In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way."
Fear over the potential of fast-follow AI remakes that might beat the copied game to market has spread among independent developers in the last few weeks. Digital Sun Games is one of several studios to cancel their upcoming public playtest for fear someone might ingest the demo into an AI tool and release their own version of its upcoming game ReVamp. Developers have also pressed Valve to explain how it can prevent the shady clones from supplanting their games on Steam, prompting the company to offer a rare explanation to developers in South Korea earlier in this week.
While developers may take some relief that Anthropic at least doesn't want to actively encourage mass game copying, this rule may only deter the most low-effort copycats. Scientists and reporters have repeatedly documented that safety limits on generative AI tools can be sidestepped by deploying rhetorical tricks. It's also unclear how the software would be able to interpret whether or not a user owns a game idea or game assets.
And as many users responding to Chasm pointed out, if Claude becomes too difficult to use, vibe-coding cloners can turn to open-weight models that have no such restrictions in place.
GameDeveloper.com has reached out to Anthropic for comment and will update this story upon its response.
Update 10/30: This story has been updated with confirmation from Anthropic.

news.title: John Romero's canceled game finds a new publisher amidst an overall scope change
news.summary_raw: John Romero's game was canceled by Xbox and his studio was on the verge of total collapse, but a new publisher has picked it up and Romero has managed to retain some of his team.

members.title: John Romero's canceled game finds a new publisher amidst an overall scope change

news.body:
Legendary game developer John Romero has managed to find a new publisher for his game after a cancellation and defunding scare earlier this summer, he told Video Games Chronicle at Gamescom Asia. While Romero has not been able to keep the entire team together, the project has been re-scoped from an intended size of over 100 people to around 15-16.
Romero's game studio, which was appropriate named Romero Games, veered toward shuttering earlier this year when employees reported that the studio was "closing down." Romero denied these reports, but did confirm that the studio's game was being funded by an unnamed publisher—which Romero said people could infer based on public information, though some of the laid off employees did name Microsoft specifically—and that funding had been suddenly pulled.
In speaking with VGC, Romero confirmed that he had to let most of the staff go as the company struggled to find a new publisher, but that "we’re just super happy."
Romero declined to name the publisher and has not officially revealed the game, though LinkedIn posts from former employees indicate that it was a shooter. The current title, Romero says, is a complete redesign of the concept, as they cannot make the same game that needed 110 people with far fewer. Romero indicates that the new smaller team size fits him better, though.
“I’ve had teams of that size [100+ staff] before, but I don’t like it when I’m just in meetings all day," he told VGC. "I like to make the game, designing by hand, and that’s what’s happening right now – making every single decision, working in Unreal Editor, making stuff, designing things, directing all the rest of the people on the team."

members.title: Maddy Makes Games removes Celeste and TowerFall from Xbox in support of pro-Palestinian BDS boycott

news.body:
Maddy Makes Games removes Celeste and TowerFall from Xbox in support of pro-Palestinian BDS boycott
Indie developers join the creators of Luck be a Landlord, Ice Water, and All Will Rise in removing games from Xbox
Indie developer Maddy Makes Games has delisted Celeste and TowerFall from Xbox to support the pro-Palestinian Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement.
According to GamesRadar, players noticed both games were removed from the platform yesterday. Maddy Thorson later confirmed this on social media.
"For those who're asking, yes we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on Xbox," Thorson wrote. "We did this to support the BDS boycott."
Maddy Makes Games is among several developers supporting the BDS boycott. Most recently, Big Walk developer House House announced it would not release its co-op game on Xbox.
"It has always been our intention for Big Walk to be played by groups of friends, and we know that keeping the game off Xbox runs counter to these intentions," the developer said.
"We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets. We've made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free."
Other developers supporting the boycott include Ice Water, creator of Tenderfoot Tactics; Speculative Agency, developer of All Will Rise; and Dan Dilorio, creator of Luck be a Landlord.
The BDS boycott was established following concerns that Microsoft's Azure and AI technologies were being used by the Israeli Ministry of Defence (IMOD) "to target civilians or cause harm in the conflict in Gaza," according to an Associated Press investigation.
Microsoft acknowledged that it provides the IMOD "with software, professional services, Azure cloud and AI services," but concluded after its own internal review that it has "no evidence to date" that its technology has "been used to target or harm people" in the ongoing conflict.

members.title: 触乐怪话：难道我真的老了

news.body:
不要啊！
最近，我提前测评了《影之刃零》。在此之前，我已经很久没有如此高强度地限时通关一个动作游戏了。赶在正式发售前打出完美结局的时候，游戏的结算页面显示我玩了47.5个小时，死亡222次。
最大的感受是腰真的很痛，手也很痛。毕竟，这款游戏的战斗着实高速，甚至在激烈的Boss战中偶尔还会夹杂QTE按键。在最终战的时候，好几个QTE需要限时连按，而我的手指已经有点按不动了，需要调动整个手腕的力气疯狂连点。至于Boss的密集程度——如果主支线一起推的话，到了一个阶段的末尾，我常常误以为自己在打连战模式。
放下手柄，我突然陷入了一种悲伤：难道我也终于到了不得不感慨“年龄到了”的时候？几年前我还能一周内通完《鬼泣5》并且没有感受到什么副作用；我还玩过首发时数值爆炸的《匹诺曹的谎言》，当时都没有感觉像现在这样精疲力尽，最多也就是骂骂咧咧而已。以前还能靠纯粹的感官刺激熬夜，如果任务链特别长还会坚持一次做完。现在如果感觉累了，就很难集中精神。
在之前的夜话中也提到，现在除了工作需求，我平时玩游戏的时候连通关强迫症也消失了。比较惊讶又合情合理的是，在访谈中遇到的一些制作人，他们也表示很少会从头到尾玩通一款游戏，绝大部分都会在摸清楚它的设计机制和基础循环之后停止，或者说暂时放下就再也没有打开过。
这和现在游戏中充斥着大量填充性内容有一定关系。人的时间精力是有限的，如果实在是对故事感兴趣，那就抽时间云一下好了。《影之刃零》让我觉得特别值当的一点是几乎没有任何填充性内容。反复跑路、刷取物资之类的几乎不存在，关卡又是线性的，对低精力人已经非常友好了。内容密集则是另一方面的事。
到头来，很长时间以来，我通关率最高、甚至会打多周目的游戏，只有很难通过“云”获得乐趣的CRPG。最近我看到有朋友在重拾旧日经典，看到他们因为剧情转折而捶胸顿足、惊讶万分的样子，好像也体会到了一点久违的快乐。
不过即使是那一类游戏，因为年代久远、机制过于繁琐等等缘故，我还是会通过打一些Mod来改善整体的游戏体验，主要是用来跳过一些“刷刷刷”内容或者不太感冒的副玩法。宗旨就是绝不折磨自己，尽量不在重复内容上浪费时间。
最后，在满意地达成了《影之刃零》的完美结局之后，这几天我又回到了《羊蹄山之魂》。不过我没怎么认真玩，只是四处逛街、看风景，甚至就牵着马站在某处旷野上挂机，自己去干别的。只能说，偶尔完全不考虑游戏本身的目的，可能才是最适合娱乐与放松的……

news.summary_raw: There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.

members.title: Gaming storefronts are facing a Slop Grenade problem | Opinion

news.body:
Gaming storefronts are facing a Slop Grenade problem | Opinion
Players and creators alike dislike AI-created games, but digital storefronts are ill-equipped for the avalanche of slop that threatens to tank discoverability and turn away consumers
There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.
At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.
This is, of course, a microcosm of broader efforts by tech giants to convince the world of the inevitability of AI permeating every facet of life and work. It follows the same playbook and rests on the same foundation of dubiously conflating many different tools and systems, including deep learning models that predate LLMs by many years, under the single banner of "AI usage".
In game development, that can mean all manner of rhetorical sleight of hand. Anything from programmers using Copilot autocompletions, to 2D artists using a background removal tool in Photoshop, to a project manager using the meeting summary tool in Zoom, can all end up counted as a tick in a box and a "studio that's using AI".
A good rule of thumb is that when someone pops up every five minutes to dramatically insist something is a fait accompli, that's a pretty sure sign that it's precisely the opposite. Nobody feels the need to convince the world of a new reality when it's actually real.
None of this is to say that plenty of developers and studios aren't experimenting with AI tools or considering how they fit their workflows. Games are a cutting-edge, high-tech industry as well as a creative one. To the extent new AI tools are useful, reliable, and effective, they'll be adopted. People will automate writing tons of boring templates or testing code, and welcome smarter tools for automating parts of the development pipeline for game assets. Nobody in a high-tech industry will turn down genuinely better versions of IDEs or image editors; that doesn't mean they want to fire their art department and replace it with half-assed prompting.
"Nobody in high-tech will turn down better versions of IDEs or image editors; that doesn't mean they want to fire and replace their art department with half-assed prompting"
Even as developers explore useful tools washed ashore amid the storm tide of hype, they're conscious of a massive factor looming over all of this. There's a reason why many dubious, anonymous surveys claim loads of development studios use AI, yet few actual studios proudly say so. Two reasons, really: first, as mentioned, many studios would probably contest that what they're doing constitutes "using AI in development" in the way people actually think of it. The second is that they know that their customers despise the idea of AI in games – a stance that has only become more deeply ingrained among consumers as AI boosters' claims of inevitability have grown more shrill.
Consumers really don't like AI, and the challenge for those hoping to change minds is that the reasons for dislike are varied and largely valid. Some dislike the aesthetic of AI-produced work – many can smell it from a mile off, and it's shocking how many ordinary folks have a viscerally negative reaction to seeing AI artwork or hearing AI-created music. Some hate the ethics of AI, with good reason; the argument for using training data to create a language model looks thin when it creates a model that mimics people's artwork, voice, or image wholesale. Others rail against data centres, economic impacts, or just hate the unlikeable billionaire figureheads of the AI wave itself.
Any attempt to normalise extensive AI usage in development will crash hard against that wall. Most consumers want art made by humans and will vote with their wallets to get it. They'll also demand the right to make informed choices, as seen with calls on Steam not only to ensure that AI-created games are clearly labelled, but that consumers have a straightforward way to filter them.
AI boosters like Epic's Tim Sweeney have railed against the labelling of AI-created titles, which is something of an admission in itself; if they were genuinely convinced that AI was poised to be embraced by the world as a valid and welcome creative tool of the future, they wouldn't be so adamant that developers must be allowed to use it under the cover of darkness.
The situation around games developed using AI extensively on the Steam platform bubbled up again a couple of weeks ago when the Steam Next Fest, an event that's meant to showcase hidden gems on the service, turned out to be riddled with lazily churned-out titles filled with AI assets.
Players demanded a strict filter to remove AI titles, a reasonable ask assuming "AI titles" can be defined meaningfully. For the broader industry, this highlights a problem with AI that's rapidly growing out of control, with far larger consequences than any debates over the creative or ethical validity of AI tools. There's an avalanche of slop bearing down on us – and nobody knows how to cope with it yet.
"Tools now churn out game after game filled with IP-infringing assets, letting those willing to pay hefty fees release several titles a week"
To see a miniature example of the chaos coming, look at retro gaming spaces now. In recent months, a niche community devoted to "decomps" – decompiling old, usually abandoned games so they can be re-implemented on modern hardware – has been overtaken by a gigantic wave of AI-driven, automated decompilations of many games, mostly still commercial titles.
These vibe-coded recreations sometimes mash bits of different games in ways that probably have corporate IP lawyers tasting colours and seeing entire new planes of reality. They remain largely a curiosity, yielding more hours of TikTok videos than playtime. However, they have drowned out that corner of the retro gaming space, likely destroying it forever – and in the process, pointed a grim finger at what's coming for other parts of the industry in the near future.
The bar to making games was already much lower than in the past, and in general, that lowering has been a good thing. High-quality development tools and the democratisation of distribution platforms have created whole new industry segments and opened doors for exciting, diverse new creative voices; it's not even worth thinking about how creatively barren videogames would have looked over the past decade without that.
What's happening now, however, is that the bar to making something that passes as a game has dropped below ground level. Tools now churn out game after game filled with IP-infringing assets, letting anyone willing to pay a hefty fee release several new titles a week.
This echoes one of the problems encountered by corporations that adopted generative AI in the past couple of years. It's called the "slop grenade" – meaning that people using AI produce massive amounts of reports, emails, and other output materials (no doubt feeling terribly productive in the process), but all of this constitutes a hand grenade of AI slop that explodes on someone else's workload, because eventually someone has to go through everything they've produced.
This is exactly what's happening to gaming storefronts – already on Steam – a massive increase in quickly produced, low-quality games given a vague sheen of professionalism by models trained on countless professionally produced video games.
Slop itself isn't a new problem, of course; anyone who watched the early promise of mobile gaming disappear under a torrent of slop knows that, as does anyone who's ever dipped a toe past the first page of Nintendo's online store. Reskins and asset flips are commonplace; many marketplaces teem with games that barely function past the first few screens or that shamelessly aim to rake in some coins from unsuspecting consumers misspelling the names of legitimate titles in their searches.
What's new is the sheer scale of what's coming – a scale at which even if every slop title only ekes out a few quid here and there, their cumulative effect could still crash discoverability, destroy marketplaces, and leech massive amounts of revenue away from real, genuine games.
Some creators are sounding the alarm about this; Smash Bros. creator Masahiro Sakurai mentioned in a recent interview that he already sees AI accelerating a flood of unoriginal titles that copy other people's ideas and fill up storefronts with games that can never be profitable. It was interesting to hear this from a Japanese developer in particular, given how positive coverage of AI has generally been in Japan compared to in Western countries.
Solutions can't come from creators; only people who can actually close the gates against the flood of slop, and it's unclear whether they have the will or means to do so.
The system right now will not cope. Platforms like Steam have largely given up on earlier attempts to gatekeep access – people hated when Steam only allowed invited titles, and still hated the greenlight system. So we've ended with what is essentially a free-for-all where any game can launch on Steam if it pays a small fee. That worked, to a degree, for a while. It's about to stop working.
"We need to stop talking about AI as an inevitable future and start talking about how to clear up the inevitable mess it's going to make"
It will stop working because even when Valve stopped holding the gate shut, a gatekeeper remained: making a game, even a bad one, took time, effort, and knowledge. members.title: 英伟达团队基于 MiniMax H3 开源视频增强方案，最高支持 4K 重生成

ai.body:
英伟达团队基于 MiniMax H3 开源视频增强方案，最高支持 4K 重生成
英伟达与麻省理工学院团队，在 Hugging Face 发布了视频增强项目 Open-H3-Regenerate-2K 的模型权重
近日，由英伟达与麻省理工学院研究人员组成的 Efficient-Large-Model 团队，在 Hugging Face 发布视频增强项目 Open-H3-Regenerate-2K 的模型权重，配套推理代码已在 NVlabs/Sana 仓库开放。该方案基于 MiniMax H3，将低分辨率视频草稿重新生成为高分辨率视频，支持 2560×1440 的 2K 输出，最高可实现 3840×2160 的原生 4K 重生成。
MiniMax H3 的完整系统包含多模态上下文处理、基础音视频生成和高分辨率重生成等环节。其中，已开放权重的 H3-Base 负责生成 768P 音视频，官方 H3-Regenerate-2K 模块通过 API 提供服务。此次发布的项目复用 H3 基础模型的生成能力，为高分辨率重生成环节提供了一套可自行部署的开放实现。
在细化模型的训练阶段，研究团队保持 H3 Transformer 主干与视频 VAE 的原有参数不变，仅训练新增的细化 LoRA。推理时，细化 LoRA 与 LightX2V FL2VA Turbo、LMS Sharp 等社区适配器合并使用，通过三步去噪，在目标分辨率下重新生成画面细节。视频草稿中的场景、布局和运动信息，则为这一过程提供基础。
为提高推理效率，项目采用社区开发的潜空间放大器，直接放大视频的潜在表示，减少高分辨率下重复解码、编码的开销。同时，方案结合 SoL-Engine 的稀疏注意力、低精度计算和快速 VAE 解码器，对细化与解码环节进行加速。
项目团队公布的测试显示，在单张 NVIDIA B200 GPU、预热后的测试条件下，一段约 5 秒视频的潜空间放大、三步细化和 2K 解码合计耗时，由未优化实现的 87.26 秒降至 22.45 秒，处理速度约为原来的 3.9 倍。其中，快速解码器将视频解码耗时从约 15 秒降至约 1.6 秒。
画质方面，项目团队在 RefinerBench-150 上进行了对比评测。在相同输入、相同 2K 输出条件下，Open-H3-Regenerate-2K 在感知质量评测 UniPercept 上的平均分为 60.0，官方 H3-Regenerate-2K API 为 53.4。VBench 评测中，该方案的美学质量、成像质量和主体一致性得分更高，官方 API 在运动平滑度和动态程度上仍略优。
MiniMax H3 在今年 8 月开放权重，围绕 H3 展开的微调、蒸馏和工具适配迅速增多，吸引了海内外研究团队与社区开发者参与，一个月内下载量超过 2400 万次，产生超过 300 个公开衍生模型，H3 成为 2026 年全球下载量最高的模型之一。
其中，英伟达与 MIT 联合围绕 H3 的开发覆盖了不同方向。除本次视频增强方案外，该团队还发布了基于 H3 Ref2VA 构建的流式视频渲染模型 StreamRender-H3，以及从 H3 视频 VAE 蒸馏而来的快速解码器 Sol-H3-VAE，分别面向交互式视频渲染和解码效率优化。
此前，LightX2V 推出的 MiniMax-H3 Turbo 提供四步、八步等蒸馏版本，社区微调模型 Singularity 则着重优化动作表现、面部细节与视觉风格。海外团队 FastVideo、Pika 也分别发布了 FastH3 四步预览版本和六步采样的 Pika H3 Flex；ComfyUI、Unsloth 则通过适配权重和量化版本，将 H3 带入更多本地创作工作流。
本文由MiniMax提供，量子位获授权转载，观点归原作者所有。

ai.body:
The October inflection point for vibe game development
28th October 2026
I’ve written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents—the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games.
- Tree Appreciator
- Emberwick
- Battle Drones
- Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
- Four times as insulting
- What happens if someone actually puts the work in?
- You should build a game!
Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:
- 3D modeling
- Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox)
- Game design (!)
That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments. The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play.
Game design is a deep subject area. I won’t pretend to be well versed in it—I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn’t think the models could do it.
Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... and it did.
In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term—no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing.
I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance.
I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.
Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.
Tree Appreciator
The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator. I used the regular Claude chat interface for this—it didn’t even need Claude Code.
I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:
Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.
I’ve found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.
This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all—I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here. Here’s the chat transcript that built it.
It’s pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.
Emberwick
This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:
Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening
Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great
Here’s that first version. It worked really well!
I was inspired to increase my ambitions:
Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that
Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village
Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll
Here’s that version.
When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way:
Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good
We’re back to prompts like “make it really good” here! Asking for a plot that “isn’t too cliche” seemed to work too—it’s a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story.
Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems—things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location.
Here’s that final game. It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through.
There’s even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features.
Once it was all working (and I’d iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I’m somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game—the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog—came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just “it’s a fantasy village and there’s a troll asleep in a cave”.
Here’s the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game.
I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here’s the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don’t think it plays nearly as well.
Battle Drones
This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week. It’s a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory.
This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what “fun” is.
The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn’t great to play.
I prompted Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun” and then later to “Port this game to three.js” and the game was transformed. There’s a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up.
Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of “mutators” that add variants of the rules.
It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here’s a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna:
Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5’s ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game.
I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache (screenshots here), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work!
Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
I live in Half Moon Bay, California, home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival, which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition.
I decided to try building a game that wasn’t just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season.
I called it “Quarter Sun Cove”.
I’m still iterating on this project, but it’s shaping up quite nicely. It’s a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off.
Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you.
It’s absurdly cute.
You can play the latest version here. I’m not convinced by the game mechanics yet—it’s actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors.
Here’s the initial brainstorming session, which resulted in this spec file. Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it.
I told Claude to “surprise and delight the user frequently” and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true.
This isn’t my best game yet—it’s not as fun to play as Battle Drones—but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal—something that wouldn’t have been built in the before-times.
Four times as insulting
If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once.
I respect those opinions
